South Carolina law sets out when a person occupying land can claim title by adverse possession, and how an owner can remove someone who has no right to be there.

What the official sources say

  • SC Code 15-67-210: occupation of premises by another is deemed in subordination to the legal title unless the premises were held and possessed adversely to the legal title for ten years before the action commenced. (S.C. Code 15-67-210; source)
  • SC Code 15-67-220 (color of title): an occupant who entered under claim of title founded on a written instrument as a conveyance, or on a court decree or judgment, with continued occupation for ten years, is deemed to have held adversely; possession of one lot is not possession of another lot of the same tract. (S.C. Code 15-67-220; source)
  • SC Code 15-67-250: for adverse possession not founded on a written instrument or judgment, land is deemed possessed only in the listed cases; a tenant's possession is deemed the landlord's possession until ten years from termination of the tenancy (or from refusal to pay rent if no written lease). (S.C. Code 15-67-250; source)
  • SC Code 27-40-430 (landlord remedy): the landlord may bring an action for possession against any person wrongfully in possession and may recover damages provided in 27-40-760(c). (S.C. Code 27-40 (section number as shown in excerpt, text preceding 27-40-440); source)

Last updated November 14, 2026.

South Carolina statutes set the basic rules between landlords and tenants, including deposits, notices and what happens when a rental is sold.

What the official sources say

  • SC Code 27-40-410(a): on termination, the security deposit must be returned less amounts withheld for accrued rent and damages; deductions must be itemized in a written notice with any amount due within thirty days after termination and delivery of possession and demand by the tenant, whichever is later. (S.C. Code 27-40-410(a); source)
  • SC Code 27-40-770(b): landlord or tenant may terminate a month-to-month tenancy by written notice at least thirty days before the termination date. (S.C. Code 27-40-770(b); source)
  • SC Code 27-40-440(a): landlord must comply with building and housing codes affecting health and safety, make repairs to keep the premises fit and habitable, keep common areas safe, supply running water, reasonable hot water and heat, and keep electrical, plumbing, heating and similar facilities in good working order. (S.C. Code 27-40-440; source)
  • SC Code 27-40-910: landlord may not retaliate by raising rent above fair-market value, decreasing essential services, or bringing an action for possession after the tenant complains to a code enforcement agency or to the landlord of a violation; remedies up to three months' rent or treble damages. (S.C. Code 27-40-910; source)
  • SC Code 27-40-420: landlord must disclose in writing at or before the start of tenancy the name and address of an owner or agent for service of process and notices. (S.C. Code 27-40-420; source)

South Carolina law requires a landlord to give a specific written notice before filing an eviction, and the number of days depends on the reason.

What the official sources say

  • SC Code 27-40-710(A): for tenant noncompliance other than nonpayment, landlord may deliver written notice that the rental agreement will terminate not less than fourteen days after receipt if the breach is not remedied in fourteen days. (S.C. Code 27-40-710(A); source)
  • SC Code 27-40-710(B): if rent is unpaid and the tenant fails to pay within five days from the date due, the landlord may terminate after written notice of nonpayment and intent to terminate; one notice, or conspicuous language in the written lease, satisfies the notice requirement. (S.C. Code 27-40-710(B); source)
  • SC Code 27-40-770(b)-(c): month-to-month tenancy ends on 30 days' written notice; a holdover tenant may be sued for possession in an action for possession. (S.C. Code 27-40-770; source)
